series.title: Tea retained for home consumption
series.unit_long: million pounds of tea retained for home consumption a year
series.label: Tea retained for home consumption (Statistical Abstract)
series.note: The whole quantity of tea retained for home consumption: in the Abstract's words, found "by deducting the Quantities Over-Entered, and those Exported subsequently to the payment of the Duties, from the Quantities Entered for Home Consumption in the first instance", from the Board of Trade's Statistical Abstracts, 1846-1938, read from the page images of eleven editions (Nos. 8, 13, 26, 41, 42, 46, 48, 59, 69 and 83); where editions overlap they agree, apart from 1865 (No. 13: 97,834,874 lb; No. 26: 97,834,600), and the latest edition read is used. Ireland is included to March 1923; from 1 April 1923 the figures exclude the Irish Free State. While the tea duty was repealed (22 April 1929 to 20 April 1932) the figures for 1929-32 are imports less re-exports. The quantity doubled between 1846 and 1865 (46.7 to 97.8 million lb), passed 200 million in 1891 and 300 million in 1913, rose from 277 million in 1917 to 388 million in 1919, and was 432 million in 1938.

series.title: Tea drunk per person
series.unit_long: pounds of tea retained for home consumption per person a year
series.label: Tea per head (Statistical Abstract)
series.note: Tea retained for home consumption (imports less re-exports) divided by the whole population, as printed by the Board of Trade; the first per-head table (No. 14, covering 1852-1866) starts in 1852. Ireland is included to 1922; from 1923 the figures are for Great Britain and Northern Ireland. None given for 1915-18. While the tea duty was repealed (1929-32) the figures are retained imports and not strictly comparable. Editions revised earlier years slightly (by up to 0.03 lb) after each census; the latest edition read is used. The 1938 figure (10.18 lb) is shown as printed but does not agree with the same edition's total retained (431.8 million lb), which gives about 9.1 lb with the population implied by the 1933-37 figures; no later edition reprints the table. From 1941 the Ministry of Food's (later MAFF's) estimated supplies per head are shown as a second line: a different measure (supplies moving into consumption; per head of the civilian population to 1947), which gives 9.3 lb for 1934-38 against 9.5 here. The Abstracts read give no figures for 1939-40. From 1974 a third line gives the tea bought for the home per person from Defra's Family Food surveys (the National Food Survey to 2000): a third measure, leaving out tea drunk outside the home, but it starts at 7.8 lb in 1974, the same as the supplies estimate, and falls to 4.2 lb in 2000 and 2.4 lb in 2024-25. Tea was rationed from July 1940 (two ounces a week, about 6.5 lb a year) to the autumn of 1952.

series.title: Tea supplies per person
series.unit_long: pounds of tea per person a year (estimated supplies)
series.label: Tea supplies per head (Ministry of Food / MAFF)
series.note: Estimated supplies of tea moving into consumption per head of population, from the Ministry of Food (the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food in the 1960 and later editions), as printed in the Annual Abstract of Statistics. Per head of the civilian population 1941-47; 1964-74 revised to the 1971 census. Editions revised single years by 0.1-0.2 lb; the latest edition read is used.

series.title: Tea bought for the home per person
series.unit_long: pounds of tea bought for the home per person a year
series.label: Tea bought for the home (Defra Family Food)
series.note: Tea brought into the home per person, from Defra's Family Food datasets: the National Food Survey (adjusted figures) for 1974-2000, then the Expenditure and Food Survey and the Living Costs and Food Survey, published in grams a person a week and shown here in lb a year (grams x 365.25/7 / 453.59). Tea bought and drunk outside the home is not included, and Defra warns that diary surveys under-report purchases. Financial years from 2001-02 are shown at the year they begin; 2006-2015 are calendar years (the financial year 2015-16 is left out, as it overlaps 2015). 67.6 g a week in 1974 (7.8 lb a year, the same as MAFF's supplies for 1974), 36.2 g in 2000 (4.2 lb), 20.7 g in 2024-25 (2.4 lb).

series.title: Price of imported tea
series.unit_long: pence per pound: average value of the tea imported, before duty
series.label: Average price of tea imported (Statistical Abstract)
series.note: The average price of all tea imported into the United Kingdom, in pence (old pence, 240 to the pound sterling) per lb, as the Board of Trade's Statistical Abstract printed it in its table of the average prices of articles imported: the value of the year's imports divided by their quantity, before duty. 1865-1870 are "from computed values" and 1871 onwards "from declared values" (the importers' own declarations), so the two parts are not strictly comparable. Read from the page images of Nos. 27, 30, 45, 46, 59 and 66; where editions overlap (1868-72, 1884-90, 1897-98, 1905-11) they agree to the hundredth of a penny. Before 1865 the Abstract gives tea prices only by country of origin (China, India, Japan), and after 1919 only for tea from India and Ceylon and from China, so neither is joined to this line. The price fell from 19.9d. a lb in 1865 to 12.6d. in 1882, 9.4d. in 1897 and 7.2d. in 1902, then rose with the war to 16.1d. in 1919.

series.title: Duty on tea
series.unit_long: pence of customs duty per pound of tea (the full rate)
series.label: Tea duty, full rate (Statistical Abstract)
series.note: The customs duty on a pound of tea, in old pence, from the Statistical Abstract's customs tariffs (the rate in force on a stated day: 31 May 1874 and 1 July 1921) and its tables of taxes reduced or increased (the date and the old and new rate of each change). Each change is drawn as a step in the year it was made. 6d. a lb on 31 May 1874; the tariffs of May 1875 and August 1889 also give 6d., and no change to the tea duty is listed between them. Cut to 4d. on 1 May 1890; 6d. from 6 March 1900; 8d. from 20 April 1904; 6d. from 1 July 1905; 5d. from 14 May 1906; 8d. from 18 November 1914; 1s. (12d.) from 22 September 1915. From 2 June 1919 tea from the British Empire paid less ("Imperial Preference"; five-sixths of the full rate in the 1921 tariff), shown as a second line. "Reduced by one-third" on 15 May 1922 (to 8d.) and "by one-half" on 5 May 1924 (to 4d.); repealed from 22 April 1929; from 20 April 1932 4d. on foreign and 2d. on Empire tea; from 22 April 1936 6d. and 4d.; from 27 April 1938 8d. and 6d. The Empire rate between 1922 and 1929 is not printed in the editions read and is left out (dotted). The duty before 1874 (it was cut in 1865, but the Abstract's table of changes gives no rates) is not shown.

series.title: Duty on Empire tea
series.unit_long: pence of customs duty per pound of tea from the British Empire (preferential rate)

series.title: Overseas trade at the prices of the time, 1854-1938
series.label: Imports
series.note: The value of goods imported into and exported from the United Kingdom each year at the prices of the time, in million pounds, from the Board of Trade's Statistical Abstracts, read from the page images of eight editions (Nos. 16, 18, 30, 33, 46, 59, 70 and 83; edition, page and table per year in the data file). Imports are valued as they arrived (cost, insurance and freight), exports as loaded on board ("free on board"); bullion and coin and goods transhipped under bond are left out. Re-exports are goods imported and sent on again ("foreign and colonial produce"), so imports less re-exports is what the country kept. Each row was checked by its own sums (United Kingdom produce + re-exports = all exports; imports less re-exports = net imports, or imports + exports = the total trade). Where editions overlap the latest edition read is used; they agree except 1870, 1885 and 1898, revised later, and 1868, where No. 18 misprints the imports (294,460,214 for 294,693,608). The values of new ships exported were not recorded in 1897-98; manufactured tobacco moved from re-exports to United Kingdom produce in 1892; from August 1914 to June 1917 goods owned by the British or Allied governments were left out; and from 1 April 1923 trade with the Irish Free State is overseas trade and the Free State's own trade is left out. Imports rose from 152 million in 1854 to 769 million in 1913 and 1,933 million in 1920, and were 920 million in 1938; exports of United Kingdom produce were 97, 525 and 471 million. Imports were above exports in every year. These are values, not volumes: for the quantities traded see "Overseas trade, 1800-1938 (at 1913 prices)".

series.title: Prices since 1800 (Retail Prices Index, long run), 1800-2025
series.label: Retail Prices Index
series.note: The ONS's long-run Retail Prices Index (series CDKO), the 'composite price index' it joins from older indexes of the cost of living to the RPI (from 1947), yearly, January 1974 = 100, on a logarithmic axis: equal steps are equal ratios. Prices in 2025 were 118 times those of 1800. Prices fell after the Napoleonic wars (16.3 in 1813, 8.4 in 1850) and moved little for a century (9.2 in 1900); they doubled in the First World War (9.8 in 1914, 19.9 in 1918) and rose to 25.3 in 1920, fell back in the 1920s and early 1930s (15.8 in 1933), and have risen in every year since 1935 but 2009: 3.6 times between 1970 and 1980, 6.0 times between 1980 and 2025.

series.title: Real wage rates, 1879-1912 and 1924-1938
series.unit_long: index of wage rates over prices
series.note: Wage rates divided by prices (the ONS's long-run Retail Prices Index): what a week's wage at the standard rates would buy. 1879-1912: the Board of Trade's index of the general course of wages (unweighted mean of building, coal mining, engineering, textiles and agriculture), 1900 = 100; 1924-1938: the Ministry of Labour's index of weekly full-time rates of wages in a representative selection of industries, 1924 = 100. Rates, not earnings: neither counts short time, unemployment, overtime or the move of workers into better-paid trades, and the two cannot be joined (no index of the same kind for 1913-1923 is open). Real wage rates rose 19% from 1879 to 1900 as prices fell (84.3 to 100), then fell to 95.7 in 1912 as prices rose; between the wars money rates fell (94.0 in 1933) but prices fell faster, so real rates rose to 110.7 in 1933 and 117.2 in 1938.

events.title: Storegga tsunami
events.text: A huge submarine landslide off Norway (the Storegga Slide) sent a tsunami across the North Sea and North Atlantic about 8,150 years ago; its sand layer lies in Scottish coastal sediments (Montrose Basin, Firth of Forth). Mosses killed by the wave date it to the coldest decades of the 8,200-year cold event.
events.citation: Bondevik, S., Stormo, S.K., Skjerdal, G. (2012) Green mosses date the Storegga tsunami to the chilliest decades of the 8.2 ka cold event. Quaternary Science Reviews 45:1-6, doi:10.1016/j.quascirev.2012.04.020

events.title: Volcanic dust veil of 536 and eruption of 540
events.text: Two large volcanic eruptions (sulfur injection 18.8 +/- 6.9 Tg S in 536 and 31.9 +/- 7.7 Tg S in 540 in HolVol v1.1) cooled Northern Hemisphere summers; Irish oak rings are exceptionally narrow and the Irish annals record a 'failure of bread' in 536-539.

events.text: Epidemic recorded by Bede in southern Britain and Northumbria and in the Irish annals from 664; part of the first plague pandemic (Justinianic). No reliable death toll.

events.title: Little Ice Age
events.text: Cool period of advanced glaciers and cold winters in Europe; start dates vary between authors (c. 1300 to c. 1550), end usually put at c. 1850-1900.

events.title: Great Famine
events.text: Harvest failures after torrential rains across northern Europe; famine and high mortality in England, Scotland and Ireland (Ireland also suffered the Bruce invasion of 1315–18).
events.citation: Jordan, W.C. (1996) The Great Famine: Northern Europe in the Early Fourteenth Century. Princeton University Press; Campbell, B.M.S. (2016) The Great Transition: Climate, Disease and Society in the Late-Medieval World. Cambridge University Press

events.title: Great Bovine Pestilence
events.text: Cattle plague (probably rinderpest) killed a large share of England's cattle and oxen, hitting ploughing and dairy food.
events.citation: Slavin, P. (2010) The Great Bovine Pestilence and its economic and environmental consequences in England and Wales, 1318-50. Economic History Review 65(4):1239-1266 (2012), doi:10.1111/j.1468-0289.2011.00625.x

events.title: Black Death
events.text: Plague (Yersinia pestis) reached Dorset in 1348, Ireland in 1348 and Scotland in 1349. Broadberry et al. estimate England's population at 4.81 million in 1348 and 2.60 million in 1351; estimates of mortality range widely, often 35–50% or more.
events.citation: Benedictow, O.J. (2004) The Black Death 1346–1353: The Complete History. Boydell Press; Broadberry, S., Campbell, B.M.S., Klein, A., Overton, M., van Leeuwen, B. (2015) British Economic Growth, 1270–1870. Cambridge University Press

events.title: Second plague outbreak (pestis secunda)
events.text: Recurrence of plague said to have struck children and young adults heavily; further outbreaks 1369 and 1375 kept population low.
events.citation: Hatcher, J. (1977) Plague, Population and the English Economy 1348-1530. Macmillan (Studies in Economic and Social History)

events.title: English sweating sickness
events.text: Recurrent epidemics of an unidentified disease in 1485, 1508, 1517, 1528 and 1551, mainly in England.

events.title: Influenza epidemic and harvest failures
events.text: Among the worst mortality crises in Wrigley and Schofield's reconstruction (from 1541): England's population fell from about 3.21 million in 1556 to 3.02 million in 1560, some 6%.
events.citation: Wrigley, E.A., Schofield, R.S. (1981) The Population History of England 1541–1871: A Reconstruction. Edward Arnold; figures as in Broadberry et al. (2015) British Economic Growth, 1270–1870. Cambridge University Press

events.title: Bristol Channel and Severn Estuary flood
events.text: On 30 January 1607 (20 January 1606/07 by the old calendar) the coasts of the Bristol Channel and Severn Estuary were flooded; estimates of the drowned range from about 500 to 2,000. Modelling supports a storm surge on a high spring tide rather than a tsunami.
events.citation: Horsburgh, K.J., Horritt, M. (2006) The Bristol Channel floods of 1607 – reconstruction and analysis. Weather 61(10):272–277, doi:10.1256/wea.133.05; RMS (2007) 1607 Bristol Channel Floods: 400-Year Retrospective (death toll range)

events.title: Great Plague of London
events.text: The last great plague epidemic in England: by 19 December 1665 the London Bills of Mortality had recorded 68,596 plague deaths, an undercount (some groups were not recorded); the true toll is often put near 100,000.

notes.title: First farmers: boom, then bust
notes.text: Radiocarbon dates from excavated sites rise sharply when farming arrives in Britain and Ireland, around 4000–3850 BC and then fall back, a boom and bust seen across north-west Europe. Scholars disagree on why: Shennan and colleagues found no link with climate, while Bevan and colleagues find that the downturns in Britain and Ireland coincide with more abrupt changes in North Atlantic climate and moves to hardier crops and more herding. The smooth HYDE population curve is a model and will not show this boom and bust; look instead for monuments begun in the 4th millennium BC in the catalogue count and for the first falls in pollen tree cover.

sources.citation: Bevan A, Colledge S, Fuller D, Fyfe R, Shennan S, Stevens C (2017) Holocene fluctuations in human population demonstrate repeated links to food production and climate. PNAS 114(49):E10524-E10531, doi:10.1073/pnas.1709190114
sources.licence: PNAS open access licence (not Creative Commons)
sources.quote: The overall summed distribution (Fig. 1C) shows a dramatic upswing in radiocarbon dates ca. 4000–3850 BCE that coincides closely with the first arrival of Early Neolithic cereal agriculture in Britain and Ireland.

sources.citation: Shennan S, Downey SS, Timpson A, Edinborough K, Colledge S, Kerig T, Manning K, Thomas MG (2013) Regional population collapse followed initial agriculture booms in mid-Holocene Europe. Nature Communications 4:2486, doi:10.1038/ncomms3486
sources.quote: We report these results for Central and Northwest Europe between 8,000 and 4,000 cal. BP and investigate the relationship between these patterns and climate. However, we find no evidence to support a relationship.

sources.citation: Bevan A, Colledge S, Fuller D, Fyfe R, Shennan S, Stevens C (2017) Holocene fluctuations in human population demonstrate repeated links to food production and climate. PNAS 114(49):E10524-E10531, doi:10.1073/pnas.1709190114
sources.licence: PNAS open access licence (not Creative Commons)
sources.quote: Major cross-regional population downturns in population coincide with episodes of more abrupt change in North Atlantic climate and witness societal responses in food procurement as visible in directly dated plants and animals, often with moves toward hardier cereals, increased pastoralism, and/or gathered resources.

notes.title: Prehistoric farmers and the woodland
notes.text: Pollen in lake and bog cores records how much of the land was wooded. Across Europe the first clear losses of broadleaf woodland follow the arrival of farming, and from about 2000 BC total forest cover moves outside its earlier range; in Britain, pollen signs of people's impact on woodland support the radiocarbon evidence for population. In the app's pollen series, tree cover in Britain falls from about half the land around 4500 BC to under a fifth by the Roman period, and in Ireland drops most after 3000 BC. The European findings are not specific to the isles; compare the tree-cover lines with the modelled cropland and pasture.

sources.citation: Fyfe RM, Woodbridge J, Roberts N (2015) From forest to farmland: pollen-inferred land cover change across Europe using the pseudobiomization approach. Global Change Biology 21(3):1197-1212, doi:10.1111/gcb.12776
sources.quote: At the European scale, the impact of Neolithic food producing economies appear to be detectable from 6000 BP through reduction in broad-leaf forests resulting from human land use activities such as forest clearance.

sources.citation: Fyfe RM, Woodbridge J, Roberts N (2015) From forest to farmland: pollen-inferred land cover change across Europe using the pseudobiomization approach. Global Change Biology 21(3):1197-1212, doi:10.1111/gcb.12776
sources.quote: Total forest cover at a pan-European scale moved outside the range of previous background variability from 4000 BP onwards.

sources.citation: Shennan S, Downey SS, Timpson A, Edinborough K, Colledge S, Kerig T, Manning K, Thomas MG (2013) Regional population collapse followed initial agriculture booms in mid-Holocene Europe. Nature Communications 4:2486, doi:10.1038/ncomms3486
sources.quote: It is important to note that strong support for these demographic patterns in Britain is found in independent evidence such as indicators of anthropogenic impact on forest cover from pollen diagrams 21 and the fluctuations in the number of directly dated cereal grains and hazel nut shells

notes.title: End of the Bronze Age: a downturn and a debate
notes.text: Radiocarbon dates from Britain and Ireland fall steeply after about 1000 BC and recover only around 400 BC. Bevan and colleagues link this to a turn towards a colder, wetter climate, but Armit and colleagues, working on Ireland, date a rapid climate shift to about 750 BC and conclude that it did not start the population collapse. The temperature series here are global or continental, so they cannot settle the question for the isles.

sources.citation: Bevan A, Colledge S, Fuller D, Fyfe R, Shennan S, Stevens C (2017) Holocene fluctuations in human population demonstrate repeated links to food production and climate. PNAS 114(49):E10524-E10531, doi:10.1073/pnas.1709190114
sources.licence: PNAS open access licence (not Creative Commons)
sources.quote: After ∼1000 BCE (the last part of the Bronze Age), there is another striking decline, and, while a higher uncertainty in the calibration curve at this point inhibits precise characterization of timing and duration, substantial recovery is visible again only by ∼400 BCE.

sources.citation: Armit I, Swindles GT, Becker K, Plunkett G, Blaauw M (2014) Rapid climate change did not cause population collapse at the end of the European Bronze Age. PNAS 111(48):17045-17049, doi:10.1073/pnas.1408028111
sources.quote: We analyze archeological 14C dates to demonstrate dramatic population collapse and present high-precision proxy climate data, analyzed through Bayesian methods, to provide evidence for a rapid climatic transition at ca. 750 calibrated years B.C. Our results demonstrate that this climatic downturn did not initiate population collapse

notes.title: 536 and after: volcanic cold
notes.text: Two large eruptions, in 536 and 540, show as tall bars in the volcanic series and are followed by a run of cold years, 536 to about 551, in the reconstructed European summer temperature (536 itself is among the four coldest summers in that series). Tree-ring scientists call the cold decades from 536 to about 660 the Late Antique Little Ice Age and link it, cautiously, to famine and plague. Irish annals record the cold of c. 536–550, and over twelve centuries Irish chronicle cold events often match eruptions in Greenland ice.

sources.citation: Sigl M, Winstrup M, McConnell JR, et al. (2015) Timing and climate forcing of volcanic eruptions for the past 2,500 years. Nature 523:543-549, doi:10.1038/nature14565
sources.quote: Our revised timescale more firmly implicates volcanic eruptions as catalysts in the major sixth-century pandemics, famines, and socioeconomic disruptions in Eurasia and Mesoamerica

sources.citation: Büntgen U, Myglan VS, Ljungqvist FC, et al. (2016) Cooling and societal change during the Late Antique Little Ice Age from 536 to around 660 AD. Nature Geoscience 9:231-236, doi:10.1038/ngeo2652 (quoted from the authors' manuscript; the published wording may differ slightly)
sources.quote: This newly defined Late Antique Little Ice Age (LALIA, 536 to ~660 CE) exceeded the LIA in severity.

Environmental Research Letters 8:024035, doi:10.1088/1748-9326/8/2/024035
sources.quote: These include the spatially extensive sixth century plague of Justinian and the severe climatic downturn expressed in Northern Hemisphere tree-rings, c.536–550 CE, both credibly reported in the Annals (Baillie 1994, McCarthy 2008 ).

notes.title: Medieval warmth to the Little Ice Age
notes.text: Worldwide, the medieval centuries were warm in some regions but cooler than today overall, and the Little Ice Age was coldest from about 1400 to 1700. In Scotland, pine tree rings show warm decades in the 1300s and a long cold spell from the 16th century to the early 1800s, though the record before about 1550 is less certain. Compare the European and Scottish summer lines with the dips in solar output and the eruptions.

sources.citation: Mann ME, Zhang Z, Rutherford S, Bradley RS, Hughes MK, Shindell D, Ammann C, Faluvegi G, Ni F (2009) Global signatures and dynamical origins of the Little Ice Age and Medieval Climate Anomaly. Science 326:1256-1260, doi:10.1126/science.1177303
sources.quote: The Medieval period is found to display warmth that matches or exceeds that of the past decade in some regions, but which falls well below recent levels globally.

sources.citation: Mann ME, Zhang Z, Rutherford S, Bradley RS, Hughes MK, Shindell D, Ammann C, Faluvegi G, Ni F (2009) Global signatures and dynamical origins of the Little Ice Age and Medieval Climate Anomaly. Science 326:1256-1260, doi:10.1126/science.1177303
sources.quote: The coldest temperatures of the Little Ice Age are observed over the interval 1400 to 1700 C.E., with greatest cooling over the extratropical Northern Hemisphere continents.

sources.citation: Rydval M, Loader NJ, Gunnarson BE, Druckenbrod DL, Linderholm HW, Moreton SG, Wood CV, Wilson R (2017) Reconstructing 800 years of summer temperatures in Scotland from tree rings. Climate Dynamics 49:2951-2974, doi:10.1007/s00382-016-3478-8
sources.quote: NCAIRN suggests that the recent summer-time warming in Scotland is likely not unique when compared to multi-decadal warm periods observed in the 1300s, 1500s, and 1730s, although trends before the mid-16th century should be interpreted with some caution due to greater uncertainty.

notes.title: Building slows when plague strikes
notes.text: Tree-ring felling dates from nearly 50,000 timber buildings in western and central Europe show building falling after each large plague outbreak, and a decline already around 1300, before the Great Famine and the Black Death. The study does not cover the British Isles, so treat it as a comparison: look for whether the catalogue's count of buildings begun per century dips in the 14th century here too. The count is by century and records surviving buildings only, so it cannot show the year-by-year pattern.

sources.citation: Ljungqvist FC, Tegel W, Krusic PJ, et al. (2018) Linking European building activity with plague history. Journal of Archaeological Science 98:81-92, doi:10.1016/j.jas.2018.08.006
sources.quote: Comparison with annual records of 9772 plague outbreaks shows that construction activity was significantly negatively correlated to the number of plague outbreaks, with the greatest decrease in construction following the larger outbreaks by three to four years after the start of the epidemics.

sources.citation: Ljungqvist FC, Tegel W, Krusic PJ, et al. (2018) Linking European building activity with plague history. Journal of Archaeological Science 98:81-92, doi:10.1016/j.jas.2018.08.006
sources.quote: Preceding the Black Death (1346–1353 CE) by five decades and the Great Famine (1315–1322 CE) by two decades, a significant decline in construction activity at c. 1300 CE is indicative of a societal crisis, associated with population stagnation or decline.

notes.title: The Great Famine, 1315–22
notes.text: Two years of almost constant rain from 1314 brought three failed harvests in a row and, with a cattle plague, the Great Famine. Broadberry, Campbell and van Leeuwen estimate that England's population fell by about an eighth by 1325, then recovered before the Black Death. The modelled HYDE population has one value per century and cannot show a shock this short; the tree-ring summer temperatures show the years themselves.

sources.citation: Slavin P (2018) The 1310s Event. In: White S, Pfister C, Mauelshagen F (eds) The Palgrave Handbook of Climate History. Palgrave Macmillan, pp. 495-515, doi:10.1057/978-1-137-43020-5_33
sources.quote: First, between approximately July 1314 and July 1316, there were twenty-four months of extreme weather, characterised by almost incessant torrential rain in summer, autumn and spring, and then frost during winter. The disastrous weather resulted in three back-to-back harvest failures and omnipresent food dearth.

sources.citation: Broadberry S, Campbell BMS, van Leeuwen B (2011) English medieval population: reconciling time series and cross sectional evidence. Working paper, University of Warwick, 3 March 2011 (the estimates were later published in Broadberry et al. (2015) British Economic Growth, 1270-1870, Cambridge University Press)
sources.quote: The Great Famine shows up as a notable negative shock with the population falling by 12 per cent to 4.12 million by 1325.

notes.title: The Black Death: fewer people, more trees
notes.text: The plague of 1348–9 cut England's population by close to half within three years, and later outbreaks kept it falling into the 15th century. Pollen records show abandoned land turning to birch and hazel scrub, with woodland greatest around 1400; in Britain, though, cereal growing had begun to fall before the plague. The modelled HYDE population and cropland for the UK both fall by more than half between 1300 and 1400. The pollen tree-cover series has values only for about 1000 and 1425, too coarse to show a short regrowth (Ireland's line rises between them, Britain's falls).

sources.citation: Broadberry S, Campbell BMS, van Leeuwen B (2011) English medieval population: reconciling time series and cross sectional evidence. Working paper, University of Warwick, 3 March 2011 (the estimates were later published in Broadberry et al. (2015) British Economic Growth, 1270-1870, Cambridge University Press)
sources.quote: The Black Death, which first struck in 1348-9 and was accompanied and reinforced by inclement weather and serious harvest failure, had a catastrophic effect, reducing the population by around 46 per cent within the space of just 3 years.

sources.citation: Yeloff D, van Geel B (2007) Abandonment of farmland and vegetation succession following the Eurasian plague pandemic of AD 1347-52. Journal of Biogeography 34(4):575-582, doi:10.1111/j.1365-2699.2006.01674.x
sources.quote: Vegetation succession on the abandoned grazing land resulted in increased cover of woody tree species, particularly Betula and Corylus, by the late 14th century. The cover of woodland was greatest at c. AD 1400, before forest clearance and agriculture increased in intensity.

sources.citation: Yeloff D, van Geel B (2007) Abandonment of farmland and vegetation succession following the Eurasian plague pandemic of AD 1347-52. Journal of Biogeography 34(4):575-582, doi:10.1111/j.1365-2699.2006.01674.x
sources.quote: In contrast, the decline in cereal production began at sites in Britain and France before the Black Death pandemic of AD 1347-52, and was probably due to the crisis in the agricultural economy, exacerbated by political instability and climate deterioration.

notes.title: Warming in central England and rising seas
notes.text: The Central England Temperature series shows the 21st century so far warmer than any period of the same length in the three centuries before, about 1.3°C above the 18th and 19th centuries. Sea level around the UK has risen about 19.5 cm since 1901, in line with the global rise. Compare the tide-gauge lines for Newlyn and Sheerness.

sources.citation: Kendon, M., Doherty, A., Hollis, D. et al. (2025) State of the UK Climate in 2024. International Journal of Climatology 45(S1):e70010, doi:10.1002/joc.70010
sources.quote: The CET series provides evidence that the 21st Century so far has overall been warmer than any period of equivalent length within the previous three centuries; 2001 to 2024 has been 1.0°C warmer than 1901–2000 and 1.3°C warmer than 1801–1900 and 1701–1800 (Table 3).

sources.citation: Kendon, M., Doherty, A., Hollis, D. et al. (2025) State of the UK Climate in 2024. International Journal of Climatology 45(S1):e70010, doi:10.1002/joc.70010
sources.quote: Since 1901, the sea level around the UK has risen by about 19.5 cm, with two-thirds of this rise happening in just over the last three decades.

sources.citation: Kendon, M., Doherty, A., Hollis, D. et al. (2025) State of the UK Climate in 2024. International Journal of Climatology 45(S1):e70010, doi:10.1002/joc.70010
sources.quote: Long-term UK sea level rise is in good agreement with the global sea level rise estimate of 20 cm (likely range 15–25 cm) for the period 1901–2018

notes.title: Scotland's ill years of the 1690s
notes.text: Tree rings from the Cairngorms make the 1690s the coldest decade of summers in Scotland's 800-year record, and the decade of the worst famine documented there. Look for the dip in the Scottish summer series and the volcanic spikes of the mid-1690s. The authors stress that cold alone does not explain the famine: how vulnerable people were and how the country responded mattered as well.

sources.citation: Rydval, M., Loader, N.J., Gunnarson, B.E., Druckenbrod, D.L., Linderholm, H.W., Moreton, S.G., Wood, C.V. and Wilson, R. (2017) Reconstructing 800 years of summer temperatures in Scotland from tree rings. Climate Dynamics 49:2951-2974, doi:10.1007/s00382-016-3478-8
sources.quote: Three of the five coldest reconstructed decades (1631–1640, 1661–1670 and 1691–1700) occurred in the seventeenth century with the 1690s representing the coldest decade in the record (Table 2). The period (~1693–1700) was marked by exceptionally cold and wet summers with widespread famine in Scotland

sources.citation: D'Arrigo, R., Klinger, P., Newfield, T., Rydval, M. and Wilson, R. (2020) Complexity in crisis: the volcanic cold pulse of the 1690s and the consequences of Scotland's failure to cope. Journal of Volcanology and Geothermal Research 389:106746, doi:10.1016/j.jvolgeores.2019.106746
sources.quote: Archival sources meanwhile reveal the 1690s as likely the worst era of crop failure, food shortage, and mortality ever documented in Scottish history. The connection appears simple - volcanic cooling triggered famine - but the drivers towards famine are far more complex.
sources.locator: Abstract (St Andrews repository; author accepted manuscript, Elsevier copyright)

notes.title: The Great Frost and Irish famine of 1740–41
notes.text: 1740 is the coldest year in the Central England Temperature series, which begins in 1659. In Ireland the cold was followed by harvest failure, famine and migration; one estimate puts the death rate as high as in the Great Famine of the 1840s. The authors argue Ireland was already highly vulnerable to famine before the frost struck.

sources.citation: Engler, S., Mauelshagen, F., Werner, J. and Luterbacher, J. (2013) The Irish famine of 1740-1741: famine vulnerability and 'climate migration'. Climate of the Past 9:1161-1179, doi:10.5194/cp-9-1161-2013
sources.quote: The "Great Frost" of 1740 was one of the coldest winters of the eighteenth century and impacted many countries all over Europe. The years 1740–1741 have long been known as a period of general crisis caused by harvest failures, high prices for staple foods, and excess mortality.

sources.citation: Engler, S., Mauelshagen, F., Werner, J. and Luterbacher, J. (2013) The Irish famine of 1740-1741: famine vulnerability and 'climate migration'. Climate of the Past 9:1161-1179, doi:10.5194/cp-9-1161-2013
sources.quote: Ó Gráda (2009) has estimated the mortality rate during the Great Frost of 1740–1741 at 13 %, compared with 12 % during the “Great Irish Famine” in the nineteenth century.

sources.citation: Engler, S., Mauelshagen, F., Werner, J. and Luterbacher, J. (2013) The Irish famine of 1740-1741: famine vulnerability and 'climate migration'. Climate of the Past 9:1161-1179, doi:10.5194/cp-9-1161-2013
sources.quote: Our analysis shows that Ireland was already particularly vulnerable to famine in the first half of the eighteenth century.

notes.title: Britain, the first big emitter
notes.text: Britain's coal-fuelled industrialisation made it the dominant source of fossil CO₂ before 1850, when the global CO₂ curve was only beginning to rise. Over 1850–2021 the UK's share of all cumulative CO₂ (including land use) is about 3%, just behind India, which is seventh.

sources.citation: Evans, S. (2021) Analysis: Which countries are historically responsible for climate change? Carbon Brief, 5 October 2021
sources.quote: Of the pre-1850 total, nearly three-quarters (2.8GtCO2) was from the UK.

sources.citation: Evans, S. (2021) Analysis: Which countries are historically responsible for climate change? Carbon Brief, 5 October 2021
sources.quote: a few European countries (which had largely cleared their land for farming before 1850) start to rise up the rankings because they were in the throes of coal-fuelled industrialisation, including France, Germany and – above all – the UK.

sources.citation: Evans, S. (2021) Analysis: Which countries are historically responsible for climate change? Carbon Brief, 5 October 2021
sources.quote: India is in seventh place in the rankings, with 3.4% of the cumulative total – just above the UK, on 3.0% – as a result of a higher contribution from land-use change and forestry.
sources.locator: Section on the top 20 cumulative emitters

notes.title: Greenhouse gases since 1750
notes.text: The CO₂, methane and nitrous oxide curves are nearly flat for millennia and then turn sharply upward after about 1750, alongside the growth of fossil-fuel emissions. The IPCC finds this rise unequivocally caused by human activities.

sources.citation: IPCC (2021) Summary for Policymakers. In: Climate Change 2021: The Physical Science Basis. Contribution of Working Group I to the Sixth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change. Cambridge University Press, doi:10.1017/9781009157896.001
sources.quote: Observed increases in well-mixed greenhouse gas (GHG) concentrations since around 1750 are unequivocally caused by human activities.

sources.citation: IPCC (2021) Summary for Policymakers. In: Climate Change 2021: The Physical Science Basis. Contribution of Working Group I to the Sixth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change. Cambridge University Press, doi:10.1017/9781009157896.001
sources.quote: Since 1750, increases in CO2 (47%) and CH4 (156%) concentrations far exceed – and increases in N2 O (23%) are similar to – the natural multi-millennial changes

notes.title: The Laki haze summer of 1783
notes.text: The Laki fissure eruption in Iceland (June 1783 to February 1784) shows as a spike in the volcanic series. Parish records suggest deaths in England in summer 1783 ran 10–20% above normal, at the same time as the sulphurous dry fog. Researchers caution that historical records alone cannot separate the effect of the pollution from those of weather and hunger.

sources.citation: Schmidt, A., Ostro, B., Carslaw, K.S., Wilson, M., Thordarson, T., Mann, G.W. and Simmons, A.J. (2011) Excess mortality in Europe following a future Laki-style Icelandic eruption. PNAS 108(38):15710-15715, doi:10.1073/pnas.1108569108
sources.quote: parish records suggest that mortality in England in the summer of 1783 was 10–20% above the 51-y moving mean

sources.citation: Schmidt, A., Ostro, B., Carslaw, K.S., Wilson, M., Thordarson, T., Mann, G.W. and Simmons, A.J. (2011) Excess mortality in Europe following a future Laki-style Icelandic eruption. PNAS 108(38):15710-15715, doi:10.1073/pnas.1108569108
sources.quote: the contribution of the volcanic air pollution to the excess mortality rates cannot be determined from historical records alone because other factors such as starvation and weather also played a role

In: Oppenheimer, C., Pyle, D.M. and Barclay, J. (eds) Volcanic Degassing. Geological Society, London, Special Publications 213:401-414, doi:10.1144/GSL.SP.2003.213.01.24
sources.quote: presents data that point to a significant increase in the national death rate in England coincident with the early phases of the eruption.

notes.title: Coal's rise and fall, and UK CO₂
notes.text: UK coal output peaked in 1913 and employment in the mines in 1920; both then fell, steeply from the 1960s. Compare the coal lines with UK fossil CO₂: emissions have fallen back to late 19th-century levels, and the decline of coal was the largest driver of that fall.

sources.citation: Ritchie, H. (2019, updated 2025) The death of UK coal in five charts. Our World in Data
sources.quote: Output grew rapidly throughout the 19th century, and peaked at 292 million tonnes in 1913.
sources.locator: Section 1, 'Coal production peaked at 292 million tonnes in 1913'

sources.citation: Ritchie, H. (2019, updated 2025) The death of UK coal in five charts. Our World in Data
sources.quote: Employment in coal peaked in 1920 at 1.19 million workers: more than 1-in-20 of the total UK workforce.
sources.locator: Section 3, 'At its 1920 peak, UK coal employed 1.2 million'

sources.citation: Ritchie, H. (2019, updated 2025) The death of UK coal in five charts. Our World in Data
sources.quote: In the last few years, UK CO2 emissions have fallen to levels last seen in the late 19th century: the decline in coal was the largest driver of this reduction.

notes.title: The Great Famine and Ireland's falling population
notes.text: Ireland's population fell sharply between the censuses of 1841 and 1851, the decade of the Great Famine of 1845–52, and in the State it kept falling until 1961. Look for the break in the Irish population line at 1851 and the long decline that follows; the State passed five million again only in 2022. The CSO figures are for the State (26 counties), not the whole island.

sources.citation: Central Statistics Office (2023) Census of Population 2022 - Summary Results: Population Changes. CSO, Cork
sources.quote: Census 2022 marked the first time in 171 years that the population of Ireland surpassed 5 million people. After a constant decline since 1851, Ireland's population recorded its lowest level in 1961 when it stood at 2,818,341.

sources.citation: Engler, S., Mauelshagen, F., Werner, J. and Luterbacher, J. (2013) The Irish famine of 1740-1741: famine vulnerability and 'climate migration'. Climate of the Past 9:1161-1179, doi:10.5194/cp-9-1161-2013
sources.quote: famine has played a more outstanding role in Irish national history than in any other European country, due to the "Great Famine" of 1845–1852 and its long-term demographic effects.

notes.title: Industrial towns, smoke and life expectancy
notes.text: Compare the rising urban share with life expectancy and coal output. Towns had long had higher death rates than the countryside, an 'urban penalty' that disappeared only in the 1930s. One study estimates that growing industrial coal use cut life expectancy by at least half a year between 1851 and 1900 (a working paper, not peer reviewed).

sources.citation: Hanlon, W.W. (2015) Pollution and mortality in the 19th century. NBER Working Paper 21647 (not peer reviewed)
sources.quote: Industrial pollution explains 30-40% of the relationship between mortality and population density in 1851-60, and nearly 60% of this relationship in 1900. Growing industrial coal use from 1851-1900 reduced life expectancy by at least 0.57 years.

sources.citation: Cambridge Group for the History of Population and Social Structure (n.d.) Migration, mortality and medicalisation: investigating the long-run epidemiological consequences of urbanisation 1600-1945 (project page)
sources.quote: The breakthrough to urban natural increase that occurred in the late eighteenth century and the eradication of the urban penalty in the 1930s mark the endpoints of major epidemiological transitions.

notes.title: Woodland's low point and the Forestry Commission
notes.text: Britain's woodland cover reached its low point, below 5%, around the end of the 19th century; the first Forestry Commission census of 1924 was made after very extensive wartime fellings. Woodland has expanded since, to 11.6% of Britain by 2000; the war had shown how quickly the country could run out of timber. Look for the turn in the woodland lines in the early 20th century.

sources.citation: Smith, S., Gilbert, J., Bull, G., Gillam, S. and Whitton, E. (2010) National inventory of woodland and trees (1995-99): methodology. Forestry Commission Research Report, Forestry Commission, Edinburgh
sources.quote: by the end of the 19th century, woodland cover had dropped below 5%. Since then Britain’s forest and woodland area has been expanding, until by the end of the 20th century there were almost 2.7 million hectares, equivalent to 11.6% woodland cover.

sources.citation: Smith, S., Gilbert, J., Bull, G., Gillam, S. and Whitton, E. (2010) National inventory of woodland and trees (1995-99): methodology. Forestry Commission Research Report, Forestry Commission, Edinburgh
sources.quote: The purpose of the Census was to assess the woodland resource after the very extensive fellings of the First World War.

sources.citation: Studholme, H. (2019) Our first 100 years sets us up for the challenges that lie ahead. Forestry England blog, 1 September 2019
sources.quote: The war had exposed that, after millennia of deforestation, the country could rapidly run out of essential timber supplies, in the event of a massive trade disruption, like a war.
sources.locator: Blog post by the Chair, paragraph 2

notes.title: The 1952 smog and the fall of sulphur dioxide
notes.text: Sulphur dioxide from burning coal contributed to the deaths in London's smog of December 1952, now estimated at about 12,000 including the months that followed. On the graphs, UK SO₂ emissions fall steeply alongside coal: official statistics put the fall since 1990 at 98%, driven by less coal burned in the energy industries.

sources.citation: Bell, M.L. and Davis, D.L. (2001) Reassessment of the lethal London fog of 1952: novel indicators of acute and chronic consequences of acute exposure to air pollution. Environmental Health Perspectives 109(Suppl 3):389-394, doi:10.1289/ehp.01109s3389
sources.quote: We estimate about 12,000 excess deaths occurred from December 1952 through February 1953 because of acute and persisting effects of the 1952 London smog.

sources.citation: Department for Environment, Food & Rural Affairs (2026) Emissions of air pollutants in the UK - Sulphur dioxide (SO2). Accredited official statistics, updated 12 February 2026
sources.quote: SO2 emitted from coal burning played a key contributory role to thousands of respiratory-related deaths during the London smog in 1952.
sources.locator: Section 1, 'What is sulphur dioxide and why are emissions of it estimated?'

sources.citation: Department for Environment, Food & Rural Affairs (2026) Emissions of air pollutants in the UK - Sulphur dioxide (SO2). Accredited official statistics, updated 12 February 2026
sources.quote: Emissions of sulphur dioxide have decreased by 98 per cent since 1990, to 84 thousand tonnes in 2024. This was driven by a decline in coal use in energy industries.
